The Duct-Tape of it's Time

Before nails, before pegs, before metal tools, people needed a way to lash together their buildings, and mount tool heads to their handles. For the fine, or light-weight jobs, animal sinews were used, but for larger tasks: twine and rope was king.

Making all kinds of cordage, from thin twines to whole ropes takes a lot of time and effort.

It's no wonder some people in the tribe would do nothing but make cordage all day long. Everything needs cordage, from nets to baskets to rugs and mats, to boats and houses, fences and leads... You really couldn't have enough of the stuff.

So how do I make it?

Many plants have the necessary fibers to become cordage, but for the purposes of this article, I'll go with what I know: Yucca.

 

  1. First thing's first, find a nice Yucca Plant and cut off a few of the lowest leaves of the plant (cutting the upper leaves damages the plant).

  2. After you have your leaves, find a nice smooth branch, and bash the entire length of the leaf until every bit of it is bruised, flip the leaf over carefully, and repeat on the other side. You do this to remove the thick skin from the inner fibers of the leaf.

  3. Once the leaf is beaten, lay it on a flat, hard surface, and carefully scrape the leaf with a wedge of wood, cleaning all the thick skin from it. Repeat this on the other side, trying not to rip the newly exposed inner fibers. Yucca Leaf Proccessing

  4. Wash the fibers out. The more of the thick dark green skin you remove from the fibers at this point, the better your cordage will be. (Of note, the sap from the leaf can be used to clean the hair and skin, although it does cause some irritation after prolonged exposure.)

  5. Lay the fibers out to dry, and process the rest of your leaves. The last thing you want is to be in the middle of making a nice piece of twine, and having to stop to make more fibers to work with.

  6. While the fibers are still damp, but not wet, you can begin the twining process:

  7. Grab a length of fiber, about half the width you want your twine to be. Hold it 2/3 the way up (yes, unevenly) with your index finger and thumb, keeping the two hanging lengths separate.

  8. Lay the lose ends across your bare thigh (you might get it to work on jeans, but skin is best for friction) again keeping the two strands separate.

  9. Lay your free hand on top of the trailing ends, palm down, and evenly roll up both ends between your hand and thigh.

  10. When the fibers try to curl up on themselves from the twisting, let go of the point 2/3 down, and keep your hand on the rolled up lengths, and allow the twisted ends to curl up on each-other. Then roll them the opposite way to make them tight and even.

  11. Grab the twine at the "Y" of the two strands with your index finger and thumb, keeping the dangling ends apart and repeat the rollign process until you start to run out of fiber on one side.

  12. Now the tricky part. You have to splice in more fiber. You can try to weave it into the short end and twist it together to hold it, or you can hold it in the "Y" while you roll the original loose ends tightly around it. I've yet to find a better method than these two options.

And then you'll have you some hand twined cordage.
